key_insight: A geographic, Optimal Transport–based distance reliably quantifies how much target regions differ from training regions and predicts cross-region model performance, enabling principled decisions about when geographic adaptation will succeed.
problem_solved: Provides a principled, quantitative way to measure domain shift across geographic regions so practitioners can predict whether a model trained in one area will generalize to another and prioritize adaptation or data collection.
method: Represent source and target geographic datasets as distributions in feature (or pixel) space and compute an Optimal Transport / Wasserstein distance between them that respects spatial structure.
Use the computed OT distance as a calibrated predictor of model performance drop (or adaptation difficulty) across regions, enabling thresholds for acceptable domain shift.
Employ scalable OT approximations and map-based visualizations to produce region-level shift scores usable for deployment planning and data acquisition.
impact: Gives ML practitioners a simple numeric signal to assess cross-region risk, optimize where to collect labels, and decide when to apply transfer or domain-adaptation methods—reducing wasted deployment effort and improving robustness for geospatial applications.
visual_elements: Choropleth/world map overlaid with OT transport flows between source and target regions (arrows sized by mass) to show where features move.
Heatmap layer of OT-derived domain-shift scores across regions (hot = high shift) for quick risk assessment.
Scatter plot of OT distance vs. model accuracy drop with regression line to illustrate predictive power of the metric.
Pipeline diagram: (data → feature extraction → OT distance computation → performance prediction → decision: deploy / adapt / collect data).
paper_title: OT on the Map: Quantifying Domain Shifts in Geographic Space
paper_authors: Haoran Zhang, Livia Betti, Konstantin Klemmer, Esther Rolf, David Alvarez-Melis
